title: Docker Complete Handbook
summary: A fundamentals-to-production guide to Docker: architecture, images and containers, Dockerfiles and build optimization, storage, networking, Compose, registries, security, debugging, orchestration, and interview prep.

chapters.title: Docker at a Glance
points: Docker packages an app and its dependencies into a portable container image that runs the same on any host
Problem it solves: 'works on my machine' drift between dev, CI and prod
Containers share the host kernel, so they start in milliseconds and use far less memory than VMs
Core objects: image, container, volume, network, registry
Handbook map: architecture, images, Dockerfile, storage, networking, Compose, registries, security, debugging, orchestration

chapters.title: Docker Architecture and Runtime Internals
points: Docker is a client-server system: the docker CLI talks to the dockerd daemon over a REST API on /var/run/docker.sock
dockerd delegates container lifecycle to containerd, which calls runc to create the container process
runc is the OCI runtime: it sets up namespaces and cgroups, then execs the process
Namespaces isolate what a process sees: pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user
cgroups limit what a process uses: CPU, memory, I/O, pids
Union filesystem (overlay2) stacks read-only image layers plus one writable layer
Container vs VM: a container is an isolated process on the shared host kernel; a VM runs a full guest OS on a hypervisor
Trade-off: containers are lighter and faster to start, VMs give stronger isolation and can run a different kernel
Example: docker run alpine echo hi, which flows CLI → dockerd → containerd → runc → process
Common mistake: assuming a Linux container can run a different kernel, or that Docker Desktop on Mac/Windows is native (it runs a hidden Linux VM)
Mounting docker.sock into a container hands that container root-equivalent control of the host
Interview Point: How does Docker differ from a VM? What do namespaces and cgroups each do? What are containerd and runc?

chapters.title: Images and Layers
points: An image is a read-only template of filesystem layers plus metadata (env, entrypoint, exposed ports)
Each Dockerfile instruction that changes the filesystem (RUN, COPY, ADD) creates a layer
Layers are content-addressed by SHA256 digest and shared between images, so they are stored and pulled once
Copy-on-write: a container gets a thin writable layer; editing a lower file copies it up first
Tag vs digest: a tag (nginx:1.27) is a mutable pointer; image@sha256:... is immutable
Image manifest lists layers and config; a multi-arch image uses a manifest list/index
Base image comparison: ubuntu (large, familiar) vs alpine (~5MB, musl libc) vs distroless (no shell) vs scratch (empty)
Example: docker pull nginx:1.27, then docker history nginx:1.27 to see layers and sizes
Example: docker image inspect shows config, layer digests and architecture
Mistake: relying on :latest, which is not guaranteed to be the newest and breaks reproducibility
Mistake: deleting a file in a later layer does not shrink the image, because the earlier layer still holds it
Interview Point: What is a layer? What is the difference between a tag and a digest? Why does a later rm not reduce image size?

chapters.title: Container Lifecycle and Runtime Control
points: A container is a running (or stopped) instance of an image with its own writable layer, network and process tree
States: created → running → paused → stopped (exited) → removed
docker run = create + start; common flags: -d, -it, --rm, --name, -p, -e, -v
PID 1 in the container is the main process; when it exits the container stops
docker stop sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after the grace period (default 10s); docker kill sends SIGKILL immediately
Resource limits: --memory 512m, --cpus 1.5, --pids-limit; exceeding memory gets the process OOM-killed
Restart policies: no, on-failure[:N], always, unless-stopped
docker exec runs an extra process in a running container; docker attach connects to PID 1's streams
docker run (new container from image) vs docker start (restart an existing stopped container)
Example: docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 --memory 256m nginx
Mistake: a shell-form CMD runs under sh, which does not forward SIGTERM, causing slow stops; use exec form
Mistake: expecting data to survive docker rm; the writable layer is deleted with the container
Interview Point: What happens on docker stop? Difference between exec and attach? Why does a container exit immediately?

chapters.title: Dockerfile Essentials
points: A Dockerfile is a text recipe of instructions that docker build turns into an image
FROM sets the base image; WORKDIR sets the working directory; COPY adds files from the build context
RUN executes at build time and creates a layer; CMD and ENTRYPOINT define the runtime command
ENV sets runtime environment variables; ARG exists only at build time
EXPOSE documents a port only; it does not publish it
USER switches to a non-root user for later instructions and runtime
CMD vs ENTRYPOINT: CMD is the default, overridable arguments; ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable, and they combine as ENTRYPOINT + CMD
COPY vs ADD: prefer COPY; ADD also extracts local tars and fetches URLs, which is surprising
Shell form (RUN npm start) vs exec form (RUN ["npm","start"]): exec form has no shell and handles signals correctly
Example: FROM node:22-alpine / WORKDIR /app / COPY package*.json ./ / RUN npm ci / COPY . . / CMD ["node","server.js"]
Mistake: forgetting .dockerignore, which sends node_modules and .git into the build context
Mistake: storing secrets in ENV or ARG, since they remain visible in docker history
Interview Point: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT? ARG vs ENV? Does EXPOSE publish a port?

chapters.title: Build Optimization and Multi-Stage Builds
points: Build cache reuses a layer if the instruction and its input files are unchanged; one miss invalidates every layer after it
Order instructions from least to most frequently changing: base, dependency manifests, install, source copy
Copy dependency manifests first, then install, then copy source, so code edits don't reinstall dependencies
Multi-stage builds: build in a fat stage, then COPY --from=builder only the artifacts into a slim runtime stage
Combine related commands in one RUN with && and clean caches in the same layer (apt-get clean, rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*)
.dockerignore shrinks the build context and avoids needless cache invalidation
BuildKit adds parallel stages, skipping unused stages, --mount=type=cache and --mount=type=secret
Comparison: single-stage (simple, huge image) vs multi-stage (small, no compilers or build tools in prod)
Example: Go app built in golang stage then copied into scratch, turning a ~800MB image into ~10MB
Example: RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip pip install -r requirements.txt
Mistake: COPY . . before installing dependencies busts the cache on every code change
Mistake: running apt-get update in its own RUN layer, which leaves a stale cached package index
Interview Point: How do you shrink an image? Why does instruction order matter? What does multi-stage solve?

chapters.title: Volumes and Storage
points: Container writable layers are ephemeral and slower; persistent data needs a volume or mount
Named volume: managed by Docker under /var/lib/docker/volumes, portable and driver-extensible
Bind mount: maps a host path into the container, ideal for live-reload in development
tmpfs mount: held in host memory only and gone on stop, good for sensitive scratch data
Comparison: volume (production data, easy backup) vs bind mount (host-path dependent) vs tmpfs (non-persistent)
Volume drivers (NFS, cloud block storage) enable shared or remote storage
A new empty named volume is populated from the image's content at that path on first mount; a bind mount hides it
Example: docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres
Example: docker run -v $(pwd):/app:ro to mount read-only
Backup pattern: run a throwaway container that tars the volume to a bind-mounted host directory
Mistake: using a bind mount in production and hitting UID/permission and path-portability problems
Mistake: docker compose down -v silently deletes named volumes and their data
Interview Point: Volume vs bind mount? How do you persist a database? What happens to data when a container is removed?

chapters.title: Docker Networking
points: Each container gets its own network namespace with a virtual interface (veth) attached to a network
bridge (default): private subnet on the host with NAT out; containers reach each other by IP
User-defined bridge adds built-in DNS, so containers resolve each other by name
host: shares the host network stack, with no isolation and no port mapping needed
none: no networking; overlay: multi-host networking for Swarm; macvlan: gives a container its own MAC/LAN address
Publishing: -p 8080:80 maps host port to container port via iptables DNAT rules
Comparison: default bridge (no name DNS) vs user-defined bridge (DNS and better isolation) vs host (fastest, no isolation)
Containers on different user-defined networks cannot talk unless attached to both
Example: docker network create app-net; docker run --network app-net --name db postgres; app connects to db:5432
Mistake: using localhost to reach another container; localhost is the container itself
Mistake: publishing a database port with -p when it only needs an internal network, which exposes it publicly
Interview Point: Bridge vs host vs overlay? How do containers find each other by name? What does -p actually do?

chapters.title: Docker Compose
points: Compose defines and runs multi-container apps from a single compose.yaml
Top-level keys: services, networks, volumes (plus configs and secrets)
A service takes image or build, ports, environment, volumes, networks, depends_on, healthcheck
Compose creates a default network per project, and service names become DNS hostnames
depends_on controls start order only; with condition: service_healthy it waits for a healthcheck to pass
Environment: env_file, ${VAR} interpolation, and a .env file for variable substitution
Profiles let you toggle optional services; override files (compose.override.yaml) layer dev settings on top
Commands: docker compose up -d, down, ps, logs -f, exec, build, config
Comparison: docker run (one container, imperative) vs Compose (declarative stack, reproducible) vs Swarm/Kubernetes (cluster scale)
Example: web + postgres + redis stack with a named volume pgdata and a healthcheck on postgres
Mistake: assuming depends_on waits until the dependency is ready
Mistake: hardcoding secrets in compose.yaml and committing them
Interview Point: What does depends_on guarantee? How do Compose services discover each other? When is Compose not enough?

chapters.title: Registries and Image Distribution
points: A registry stores and serves images; a repository holds the versions (tags) of one image
Image reference format: registry/namespace/repo:tag, and Docker Hub is the default registry
Workflow: docker login, docker tag, docker push, docker pull
Pushes upload only layers the registry does not already have, and pulls fetch only missing layers
Public vs private registries: Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR, GCR/Artifact Registry, ACR, self-hosted registry:2 or Harbor
Comparison: Docker Hub (public default, pull rate limits) vs cloud registry (IAM-integrated, near the workload) vs Harbor (self-hosted, scanning and replication)
Tagging strategy: semantic versions plus the git SHA for traceability; pin deployments by digest
Pull-through cache or mirror reduces rate-limit pain and speeds CI
Example: docker tag app:1.4.2 ghcr.io/acme/app:1.4.2 && docker push ghcr.io/acme/app:1.4.2
Example: multi-arch build with docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push
Mistake: deploying :latest and being unable to tell or roll back what version runs
Mistake: pushing images with baked-in secrets to a public repository
Interview Point: What is the difference between a registry and a repository? How do you version images? How do you speed up pulls?

chapters.title: Docker Security
points: Containers are isolated processes, not a hard security boundary: a kernel exploit affects the host
Run as non-root with USER; by default container root is UID 0 on the host unless user namespaces remap it
Drop capabilities: --cap-drop ALL then add only what is needed; avoid --privileged
Use --read-only filesystems with tmpfs for writable paths, and --security-opt no-new-privileges
Seccomp and AppArmor/SELinux profiles restrict system calls and file access
Minimal images (distroless, alpine) reduce attack surface and CVE count
Scan images (Trivy, Docker Scout, Grype) in CI; pin versions and rebuild regularly for patches
Secrets: use BuildKit --mount=type=secret at build time and Docker/Swarm/Kubernetes secrets at runtime, not ENV or image layers
Comparison: rootful daemon (default, bigger blast radius) vs rootless mode / Podman (daemon and containers run as an unprivileged user)
Sign and verify images (Docker Content Trust, cosign) to protect the supply chain
Mistake: mounting /var/run/docker.sock or running --privileged for convenience
Mistake: using unpinned images from unknown publishers
Interview Point: Are containers secure by default? How do you handle secrets? What does --privileged do?

chapters.title: Debugging and Troubleshooting
points: First step: docker ps -a to see state and exit code, then docker logs --tail 100 -f <container>
Exit codes: 0 clean, 1 app error, 125 daemon error, 126 not executable, 127 command not found, 137 SIGKILL/OOM, 143 SIGTERM
docker inspect gives config, mounts, networks, IPs, State.OOMKilled and health status
docker exec -it <c> sh to explore a running container; for a crash-looping one, override the entrypoint with --entrypoint sh
docker stats shows live CPU, memory and I/O; docker top lists processes; docker events streams daemon events
Networking checks: docker network inspect, test DNS and ports from inside the container with curl, nslookup or nc
Build debugging: docker build --progress=plain --no-cache, and target a stage with --target
Disk full: docker system df shows usage; docker system prune (add --volumes carefully) reclaims space
Comparison: logs (what the app said) vs inspect (how it was configured) vs exec (live state)
Example: container exits 137, so check docker inspect for OOMKilled=true and raise --memory or fix the leak
Mistake: debugging inside a container and expecting manual fixes to persist, since they vanish on recreate
Mistake: running prune -a --volumes on a host holding needed data
Interview Point: A container keeps restarting; how do you diagnose it? What does exit code 137 mean? How do you debug a failing build?

chapters.title: Production and Orchestration
points: Production needs more than docker run: scheduling, scaling, self-healing, rolling updates, service discovery and secrets
Healthchecks (HEALTHCHECK or Compose healthcheck) let orchestrators detect and replace unhealthy containers
Set restart policies, resource limits and log rotation (json-file max-size/max-file or a central driver)
Design for statelessness: keep state in volumes or external databases, and config in environment or secrets
Handle SIGTERM for graceful shutdown and use an init process (--init, tini) to reap zombie processes
Docker Swarm: built-in orchestration with services, replicas, overlay networks and rolling updates; simple but a smaller ecosystem
Kubernetes: the industry-standard orchestrator with pods, deployments, services, ingress and autoscaling; more powerful and more complex
Comparison: Compose (single host) vs Swarm (small clusters, simple) vs Kubernetes (large scale, rich ecosystem)
Rollout strategies: rolling update, blue/green and canary, with image tags immutable per release
Example: docker service create --replicas 3 -p 80:80 nginx, then docker service update --image nginx:1.27 for a rolling update
Mistake: running stateful databases in containers without durable volumes and backups
Mistake: no resource limits, so one noisy container starves the host
Interview Point: Why use an orchestrator? Swarm vs Kubernetes? How do you do zero-downtime deploys?

chapters.title: Interview Questions and Best Practices
points: Q: Container vs image? An image is the immutable template; a container is a running instance of it
Q: How do you reduce image size? Slim or distroless base, multi-stage builds, .dockerignore, merged and cleaned RUN layers
Q: How is data persisted? Named volumes or bind mounts, never the writable layer
Q: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT, and COPY vs ADD? Answer with default-args vs fixed executable, and prefer COPY
Q: How do containers communicate? A user-defined network with DNS by service name
Q: How do you secure containers? Non-root, dropped capabilities, read-only filesystem, scanned and pinned images, proper secrets handling
Best practice: one process concern per container, with config via environment
Best practice: pin base image versions or digests and rebuild regularly
Best practice: log to stdout/stderr and let the platform collect it
Best practice: keep images small, reproducible and tagged immutably
Mistake: treating containers like pets by patching them in place instead of rebuilding
Interview Point: Walk through containerizing an app end to end, from Dockerfile to deployment, and explain each choice

chapters.title: Docker Cheatsheet
points: Run: docker run -d --name n -p 8080:80 -v vol:/data --network net image
Inspect: docker ps -a, logs -f, inspect, stats, top, exec -it c sh
Lifecycle: docker start, stop, restart, kill, rm -f, pause, unpause
Images: docker build -t name:tag ., images, history, tag, push, pull, rmi
Cleanup: docker system df, container/image/volume/builder prune, system prune
Volumes and networks: docker volume create/ls/inspect, docker network create/ls/inspect/connect
Compose: docker compose up -d --build, down, ps, logs -f, exec, config
Dockerfile skeleton: FROM, WORKDIR, COPY manifests, RUN install, COPY src, USER, EXPOSE, CMD exec form
Exit codes: 137 = killed/OOM, 143 = SIGTERM, 127 = command not found
Security checklist: non-root, cap-drop ALL, read-only, scan, pin, no docker.sock
